prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the development of long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonists that transformed treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: The round-1 exchange confirms that B007 is a single, mature part on which all six of us agree on science, maturity and the first two names. The disagreement is one principle: whether the prize names the physiology or the physiology and the step that made it a medicine. I resolve it in favour of the second reading, and I state the principle so it is not a default. Holst and Drucker are credited for the physiology and biology of GLP-1. Knudsen is credited for a specific, documented, original step, fatty-acid acylation for albumin binding that gave once-daily and then once-weekly dosing. That step is what carried the physiology into the outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease that make this achievement exceptional. A citation that names both halves is accurate for all three people and does not need to rule on who first identified the active peptide.
statement.case_against: I take the strongest objection from Perlmann, Wahren-Herlenius and Linnarsson to be that the prize rewards a discovery and not a product, and that Knudsen's work is development that rests on the identification of the active peptide. That is a real argument and I have not defeated it. Omitting Mojsov can be read as settling a contested priority question without evidence, and including Knudsen in preference to her can be read as favouring an industrial scientist over a discoverer. I cannot verify either claim beyond the supplied credit. Four of six colleagues hold the other configuration, and I recognise that the prize would be defensible with Mojsov in the third place. Long-term safety and durability of obesity treatment are also still accruing, which does not change my ranking.

responses.point: Perlmann holds Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, arguing that the Nobel Prize rewards a discovery and not a product, that Knudsen's work builds on identification of the active peptide, and that contested priority is a reason for care and not exclusion.
responses.response: I accept that discovery-first is the default principle and that a contested priority calls for care. My disagreement is with the claim that acylation is engineering that merely follows the peptide work. Making a native peptide with a half-life of minutes into a once-weekly drug required a new mechanistic idea about albumin binding, and the Medicine prize has recognised such enabling steps before. I also see the risk in the way you put it. Excluding Mojsov settles priority against her without evidence, and including her settles it for her on a credit no one in this committee has checked, so the argument is symmetric and does not by itself decide the third name. My position stays because Knudsen's contribution is documented in approved drugs and Mojsov's weight cannot be tested from this record. I would move if the committee judged the active-peptide identification to be the decisive step, and I do not hold that view lightly.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius supports Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, holds that the citation should name the physiology, and says dropping Mojsov settles the uncertainty against her without evidence while she would reopen the question if the committee wants drug development honoured.
responses.response: You say you would reopen the choice if the committee wants the prize to honour drug development explicitly, and that is the question I think we should decide in round 2. I answer yes for this prize, because the achievement that sets B007 apart from the other shortlisted candidates is that the physiology reached patients and was then proven in randomised outcome trials. A citation that stops at the hormone describes only the first half of that. I agree that leaving out Mojsov does not remove the uncertainty about priority. For that reason I would word my citation so that it makes no claim about who identified the active form, and rests only on the physiology of GLP-1 and the development of long-acting agonists. I accept that Habener's absence from the supplied credit limits what any wording can claim on the Mojsov side too.

responses.point: Linnarsson favours Drucker, Holst and Mojsov with a discovery-centred citation, and says the outcome depends on whether the prize rewards physiology or development, while worrying that B007 is so far ahead that credit allocation may not be tested hard enough.
responses.response: Your last concern is fair and it is why I have not simply accepted the majority trio. The credit allocation should be tested, and my test is whether each name can be tied to a specific, checkable contribution in the supplied record. Holst, Drucker and Knudsen pass that test. Mojsov's contribution is real, but its priority is contested and neither of us can resolve it here. I also take your point that a discovery-centred citation is safer on the Habener limit. Where I differ is that a prize reading as physiology only would leave out the reason the field is being honoured at all, which is the medicines. If the committee decides on your principle, I would not obstruct the Mojsov trio, but I would want the record to show that the choice was a judgement on principle and not a verdict on Knudsen's contribution.

responses.point: Sandberg shares the Drucker, Holst and Knudsen configuration and asks the committee to state the principle explicitly, so that the trio does not look like an unexplained exclusion of Mojsov, while saying he would accept the Mojsov trio if the committee wants a purely discovery-level prize.
responses.response: You are right that two of us agreeing by default is not an argument, and I have tried to state the principle above. Holst and Drucker are named for the physiology, and Knudsen is named for the translation into usable agonists, and the citation says both. I do not think the principle is cost-free. It prefers a documented development step over a disputed discovery credit, and a colleague who weights discovery-level priority above all would reasonably reverse that. I differ from you only in that I am not prepared to call the Mojsov trio a lesser prize. It would be a coherent prize under a different principle, and I would vote for the best-supported version of either once the committee has chosen.

uncertainties: Whether the committee adopts a discovery-only principle for B007, which favours Mojsov, or a discovery-and-development principle, which favours Knudsen.
Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide relative to Habener and others, which I cannot verify from the supplied record.
For the alternatives, whether the Eshhar originator question can be handled within three names for B041, and whether the indirect clinical consequence of B004 is acceptable.
Whether a two-part configuration is feasible. B007 needs all three names, so I treat the prize as a single part.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate. I disclosed a postdoctoral period with Paul Greengard and co-authored work with committee colleague Thomas Perlmann on dopamine-neuron topics. Neither involves a credited name on any shortlisted ballot, and nothing in round 1 has changed that. I do not need to recuse myself.
